Dynamical signatures of deconfined spinons in dimerized sawtooth chains

Nishan Ranabhat Email: uve4wq@virginia.edu Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, Virginia 22904, USA    Brandon B. Le Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, Virginia 22904, USA    Seung-Hun Lee Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, Virginia 22904, USA    Gia-Wei Chern Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, Virginia 22904, USA
August 26, 2026
Abstract

We study the ground-state properties and dynamical response of the Heisenberg model on the sawtooth chain in and away from the exactly solvable valence-bond-solid (VBS) point. We employ U(1)-symmetric density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) and time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) methods to compute equilibrium diagnostics and the zero-temperature dynamical structure factor (DSF) Sz​z​(q,ω)S^{zz}(q,\omega) across the dimerized phase, a valence-bond-ordered state in which the two symmetry-equivalent apex–base bonds of each triangle develop unequal spin correlations, probing the approach to the continuous lower phase boundary, the exact VBS point, and the approach to the first-order upper boundary. In every regime, the DSF is a broad continuum dominated by a bright band at its lower edge, with the intensity at the one-triplon energy ω≃JA​B\omega\simeq J_{AB} suppressed. We identify the spectrum as a deconfined two-spinon continuum of kink and antikink domain walls between the two degenerate singlet coverings. Closed-form spinon dispersions fix the continuum edges and track the dominant band across the zone in all three regimes, while an explicit finite-separation two-kink calculation in a constrained Hilbert space reproduces the measured intensity distribution. Our results provide a microscopic picture of fractionalized excitations in the dimerized sawtooth chain and are relevant to the recently discovered Ti3+ kagome fluorides, where strongly anisotropic exchange interactions can generate sawtooth-chain building blocks.

I Introduction

Competing exchange interactions on geometrically frustrated lattices generate some of the richest collective behavior in condensed matter: fractionalized excitations, macroscopically degenerate ground-state manifolds, and exotic ordered and disordered phases. Quantum fluctuations are particularly strong in one dimension, where they can preclude magnetic order and lead to elementary excitations with fractional quantum numbers. The antiferromagnetic sawtooth chain, which is a line of corner-sharing triangles, combines these one-dimensional quantum effects with geometric frustration and provides a tractable setting in which dimerization and fractionalized excitations can be studied microscopically. This geometry is realized in real materials, including the natural mineral atacamite, Cu2Cl(OH)3 [18], high-spin molecular rings [3], and, more recently, Ti3+ kagome fluorides [43].

The sawtooth chain (Fig. 1) has two spin-1/21/2 sites per unit cell: a basal/chain spin 𝐒iB\mathbf{S}^{B}_{i} and an apical spin 𝐒iA\mathbf{S}^{A}_{i}, for i=1,…,Li=1,\ldots,L unit cells (N=2​LN=2L spins). With apex-base coupling JA​BJ_{AB} and base-base coupling JB​BJ_{BB}, the Hamiltonian is

H=JB​B​∑i=1L−1𝐒iB⋅𝐒i+1B+JA​B​∑i=1L𝐒iA⋅𝐒iB+JA​B​∑i=1L−1𝐒iA⋅𝐒i+1B,H=J_{BB}\sum_{i=1}^{L-1}\mathbf{S}^{B}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}^{B}_{i+1}+J_{AB}\sum_{i=1}^{L}\mathbf{S}^{A}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}^{B}_{i}+J_{AB}\sum_{i=1}^{L-1}\mathbf{S}^{A}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}^{B}_{i+1}, (1)

i.e., each apex couples to the two basal spins of its triangle, and consecutive basal spins couple along the chain. The single control parameter is the ratio r≡JB​B/JA​Br\equiv J_{BB}/J_{AB} which can also be viewed as a frustration parameter. At r=0r=0 the basal bonds vanish and Eq. (1) reduces to the uniform, unfrustrated S=1/2S=1/2 Heisenberg chain of N=2​LN=2L spins with exchange JA​BJ_{AB}, whereas at r=1r=1 all three bonds of every triangle are equal and the frustration within each triangle is maximal. As rr varies at fixed antiferromagnetic sign, the ground state passes through three regimes [4, 20, 31]. At small rr (r≲0.49r\lesssim 0.49), it is gapless and adiabatically connected to the r=0r=0 Heisenberg chain, whose dynamics is characterized by the des Cloizeaux–Pearson two-spinon continuum [9, 27]. At intermediate rr (0.49≲r≲1.50.49\lesssim r\lesssim 1.5), the system enters a gapped dimerized phase: a valence-bond-ordered state in which the two symmetry-equivalent apex-base bonds of each triangle develop unequal spin correlations. This bond order is static, the two bond energies are fixed ground-state expectation values whose inequality breaks the mirror symmetry between the two bonds. Away from r=1r=1, the ground state is a dressed superposition of many singlet configurations rather than a product of isolated dimers, yet the average apex-base bond contrast remains finite. The phase contains the exact valence-bond-solid (VBS) point r=1r=1, where the bond contrast is maximal, and the ground state is a tensor product of apex-base singlets. At large rr (r≳1.5r\gtrsim 1.5), it enters a gapless noncollinear phase through a first-order transition [31]. In this work, we study the dimerized phase, including both its equilibrium properties and its full dynamical response.

The Ti3+ (3​d13d^{1}, S=1/2S=1/2) kagome fluorides [13, 21, 22] have recently emerged as a family of frustrated magnets that interpolates between near-ideal kagome lattices and networks with strongly anisotropic exchange interactions. Density-functional theory calculations on these materials find strongly bond-dependent exchange interactions that, in the more distorted members, naturally generate linear and sawtooth (Δ\Delta)-chain motifs [19, 41]. Neutron scattering measurements on the modulated kagome antiferromagnet Cs8RbK3Ti12F48 revealed a gapless dispersive continuum indicative of fractionalized excitations [42], while recent measurements on its sister compound Cs8LiNa3Ti12F48 [43, 2] further point to strongly anisotropic magnetic interactions. These developments motivate a microscopic understanding of the spin-1/21/2 sawtooth chain, not only as a paradigmatic frustrated one-dimensional system, but also as a building block relevant to this new class of Ti-based kagome magnets.

The VBS point (r=1r=1) of the dimerized phase has been well studied [28, 37, 16]: the ground state is an exact tensor product of apex-base singlets, and the elementary excitations are gapped kink and antikink spinons. A local spin excitation, however, carries Δ​S=1\Delta S=1 and can also be viewed as creating an on-dimer triplet. This raises a basic question for the dynamical response: whether the spectral weight is governed by a coherent triplon excitation or by its fractionalized spin-1/21/2 constituents. Away from the solvable point, variational estimates of the antikink dispersion have been obtained [29], but the dressed regimes r≠1r\neq 1 remain largely unexplored, both in their ground-state properties and in their dynamical response.

The natural probe of the latter is the dynamical structure factor (DSF; see Sec. II.2), the momentum- and energy-resolved spin response measured directly by inelastic neutron scattering. A complete map of the zero-temperature Sz​z​(q,ω)S^{zz}(q,\omega) across the dimerized phase, and with it the identification of the physical origin of its dominant low-energy excitations, remains unstudied. In particular, it remains unclear how the kink–antikink description at the exactly solvable VBS point evolves away from r=1r=1, and whether fractionalized spinons continue to control the dynamical response throughout the dimerized phase. Addressing this question also traces how the dynamics evolves between the two distinct limits that bound the dimerized phase.

Methodologically, we employ a combination of tensor-network algorithms for ground-state and real-time dynamics [45, 35, 14, 7], variational probes [11, 12, 1, 39], and effective domain-wall analysis [16, 28, 37], akin to the recent study of partially dimerized J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} chains [39]. Building on this toolkit, we compute and interpret the full zero-temperature longitudinal dynamical structure factor Sz​z​(q,ω)S^{zz}(q,\omega) of the dimerized sawtooth chain at three representative points, r=0.72r=0.72, 1.001.00, and 1.381.38, chosen to probe the approach to the lower continuous boundary, the exact VBS point, and the approach to the upper first-order boundary, respectively. We find that the dynamical response throughout the dimerized phase is dominated not by a coherent one-triplon mode, but by a broad two-spinon continuum formed by deconfined kink and antikink domain walls. Closed-form spinon dispersions determine the continuum boundaries and track its dominant low-energy spectral features, while an explicit finite-separation two-kink construction reproduces the distribution of spectral weight within the continuum.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the numerical and analytical methods. Section III.1 presents the equilibrium ground-state characterization, while Secs. III.2–III.4 present the dynamical structure factor and its two-spinon interpretation. Technical details are provided in Appendixes A–D.

II Methods

Our numerical approach combines three complementary methods built around a matrix-product-state (MPS) representation of the many-body wave function. We first use the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) to obtain accurate ground states and characterize their equilibrium properties. Starting from these ground states, we then employ the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) to simulate the real-time evolution following a local spin excitation, from which the dynamical structure factor Sz​z​(q,ω)S^{zz}(q,\omega) is obtained. We further use a numerical single-mode approximation (SMA), constructed directly from the DMRG ground state, as an independent variational probe of the excitation spectrum. These MPS-based methods are complemented by a semi-analytical finite-DD two-kink construction, anchored by brute-force exact diagonalization, which resolves the distribution of spectral weight within the dynamical continuum. Together, these methods provide complementary access to the ground-state properties, the full dynamical response, and the low-energy excitation spectrum of the sawtooth chain.

II.1 Ground state from DMRG

All tensor-network calculations use U⁡(1)U(1)-symmetric, block-sparse MPS tensors that explicitly conserve StotzS^{z}_{\rm tot}. Ground states are obtained with the two-site density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) algorithm [45, 35] in the Stotz=0S^{z}_{\rm tot}=0 sector. We consider two system sizes with open boundary conditions (OBC): L=64L=64 to study the equilibrium ground-state properties (see Sec. III.1), and L=32L=32 to generate the ground states that enter the dynamical structure factor (DSF) protocol of Sec. II.2. The two-site update grows the bond dimension adaptively up to χDMRG=128\chi_{\rm DMRG}=128, with SVD truncation cutoffs of 10−810^{-8}–10−1010^{-10}. The quality of the converged states is tested by the energy variance per site, v=(⟨H2⟩−E02)/N​JA​B2v=(\expectationvalue{H^2}-E_{0}^{2})/NJ_{AB}^{2}, evaluated on the final MPS (v=0v=0 for an exact eigenstate). For the L=64L=64 states, v=6.0×10−11v=6.0\times 10^{-11} for r=0.72r=0.72 and v=5.8×10−9v=5.8\times 10^{-9} for r=1.38r=1.38, while for r=1r=1 DMRG reproduces the exact valence-bond-solid ground state, E0=−34​L​JA​BE_{0}=-\tfrac{3}{4}LJ_{AB}, to machine precision (v≲10−14v\lesssim 10^{-14}). For L=32L=32, vv is marginally smaller for all three cases. Further details on the convergence and errors in DMRG are provided in Appendix A.

II.2 Dynamical structure factor protocol

We compute the zero-temperature DSF, defined as the space-time Fourier transform of the dynamical spin-spin correlator,

Sz​z​(q,ω)=∫−∞∞d​t​ei​ω​t​1N​∑j,le−i​q​(rj−rl)​⟨Sjz​(t)​Slz​(0)⟩,S^{zz}(q,\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\!\!dt\;e^{i\omega t}\,\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j,l}e^{-iq(r_{j}-r_{l})}\,\langle S^{z}_{j}(t)\,S^{z}_{l}(0)\rangle, (2)

with Sjz​(t)=ei​H​t​Sjz​e−i​H​tS^{z}_{j}(t)=e^{iHt}S^{z}_{j}e^{-iHt} and the expectation taken in the DMRG ground state |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle. The DSF is directly accessible in inelastic neutron scattering experiments [42]. Its real-time formulation also provides a natural route for its calculation within the MPS framework. Acting with a local spin operator on the ground state creates a localized excitation containing the many-body eigenstates that couple to this probe. The subsequent real-time evolution encodes their energies and propagation, which are resolved in momentum and frequency through Fourier transformation. We carry out this evolution using two-site TDVP, which projects the Schrödinger equation onto the MPS variational manifold while allowing the bond dimension to grow as entanglement develops during the time evolution.

With the ground state available, the protocol for calculating the DSF is as follows: a single SzS^{z} operator is applied at the central cell j0=L/2j_{0}=L/2, separately on each sublattice site σ∈{B,A}\sigma\in\{B,A\}, |ϕσ⟩=Sσ,j0z​|Ψ0⟩|\phi^{\sigma}\rangle=S^{z}_{\sigma,j_{0}}|\Psi_{0}\rangle. The real-time evolution of each source is then |ϕσ​(t)⟩=e−i​H​t​|ϕσ⟩|\phi^{\sigma}(t)\rangle=e^{-iHt}|\phi^{\sigma}\rangle [14, 7]. We use a maximum bond dimension χTDVP=600\chi_{\rm TDVP}=600 and a time step Δ​t=0.01​JA​B−1\Delta t=0.01\,J_{AB}^{-1}, evolving up to the final time tfinal=8​JA​B−1t_{\rm final}=8\,J_{AB}^{-1}. The truncation is monitored through the cumulative discarded Schmidt weight, which stays below 7.5×10−47.5\times 10^{-4} in the least favorable channel. Further details on the errors incurred in the TDVP calculation are provided in Appendix A. Measuring SzS^{z} on every cell jj and sublattice σ′\sigma^{\prime} against the evolved source gives the real-space Green’s function

Gσ′​σ​(j,t)\displaystyle G^{\sigma^{\prime}\sigma}(j,t) =⟨Ψ0|Sσ′,jz​(t)​Sσ,j0z​(0)|Ψ0⟩\displaystyle=\langle\Psi_{0}|\,S^{z}_{\sigma^{\prime},j}(t)\,S^{z}_{\sigma,j_{0}}(0)\,|\Psi_{0}\rangle (3)
=⟨Ψ0|ei​H​t​Sσ′,jz​e−i​H​t​Sσ,j0z|Ψ0⟩\displaystyle=\langle\Psi_{0}|e^{iHt}\,S^{z}_{\sigma^{\prime},j}e^{-iHt}\,S^{z}_{\sigma,j_{0}}\,|\Psi_{0}\rangle
=ei​E0​t​⟨Ψ0​|Sσ′,jz|​ϕσ​(t)⟩\displaystyle=e^{iE_{0}t}\langle\Psi_{0}|\,S^{z}_{\sigma^{\prime},j}\,|\phi^{\sigma}(t)\rangle

in the four sublattice channels (σ′,σ)∈{B,A}2(\sigma^{\prime},\sigma)\in\{B,A\}^{2}. Finally, we perform a double Fourier transform of Gσ′​σ​(j,t)G^{\sigma^{\prime}\sigma}(j,t) and sum over the sublattice contributions, Sz​z​(q,ω)=1N​∑σ′​σSσ′​σ​(q,ω)S^{zz}(q,\omega)=\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{\sigma^{\prime}\sigma}S^{\sigma^{\prime}\sigma}(q,\omega), to evaluate Eq. (2). Accounting for the relative positions of the two sublattices, with δB=0\delta_{B}=0 and δA=12\delta_{A}=\tfrac{1}{2}, places the DSF in the extended Brillouin-zone convention q∈[0,4​π]q\in[0,4\pi] used throughout.

II.3 Numerical single-mode approximation

We complement the full numerical dynamical response calculated via TDVP with an independent variational estimate of the low-energy excitation spectrum. The single-mode approximation constructs a restricted variational space of excited states by acting on the ground state with a chosen set of local operators. Here we implement a multi-operator SMA [11, 12, 1], in the matrix-valued form of Ref. [39], directly on the MPS-based DMRG ground state |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle, retaining separate local spin operators on the two sublattices of the sawtooth chain.

The two local SzS^{z} probes per cell, {ΩiB=SBiz,ΩiA=SAiz}\{\Omega^{B}_{i}=S^{z}_{B_{i}},\,\Omega^{A}_{i}=S^{z}_{A_{i}}\}, span the 2​L2L-dimensional space of mutually nonorthogonal trial states |ϕiσ⟩=Ωiσ​|Ψ0⟩|\phi_{i}^{\sigma}\rangle=\Omega^{\sigma}_{i}|\Psi_{0}\rangle. The variational spectrum follows from the single real-space generalized eigen-problem,

H~​|ψ⟩=ω​𝒪​|ψ⟩,\tilde{H}\,|\psi\rangle=\omega\,\mathcal{O}\,|\psi\rangle, (4)

with overlap 𝒪i​jσ​σ′=⟨Ψ0|(Ωiσ)†​Ωjσ′|Ψ0⟩\mathcal{O}^{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}_{ij}=\langle\Psi_{0}|(\Omega^{\sigma}_{i})^{\dagger}\Omega^{\sigma^{\prime}}_{j}|\Psi_{0}\rangle and H~i​jσ​σ′=⟨Ψ0|(Ωiσ)†​(H−E0)​Ωjσ′|Ψ0⟩\tilde{H}^{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}_{ij}=\langle\Psi_{0}|(\Omega^{\sigma}_{i})^{\dagger}(H-E_{0})\Omega^{\sigma^{\prime}}_{j}|\Psi_{0}\rangle, built by sandwiching the Hamiltonian MPO between the corresponding MPS states. Since OBC break exact translation symmetry, momentum is assigned a posteriori: each eigenvector is projected onto the plane-wave combinations |k,σ⟩=L−1/2∑je−i​k​jΩjσ|Ψ0⟩|k,\sigma\rangle=L^{-1/2}\sum_{j}e^{-ikj}\Omega^{\sigma}_{j}|\Psi_{0}\rangle on the grid k=2​π​m/Lk=2\pi m/L (m=0,1,…,L−1m=0,1,\ldots,L-1) and labeled by the momentum of maximal weight. The lowest eigenvalue at each kk defines the variational SMA dispersion [black points in Fig. 4(b),(d),(f)] and provides a variational estimate of the lowest excitation accessible within this local-operator subspace. At the exact VBS point, r=1r=1, the SMA reproduces the flat triplon at ω=JA​B\omega=J_{AB}. Regularization of the near-singular metric and filtering of the spurious U⁡(1)U(1) null mode are detailed in Appendix B.

II.4 Finite-DD two-kink construction and exact diagonalization

To resolve how the spectral weight is distributed within the dynamical continuum, we diagonalize the effective two-spinon (kink-antikink) problem directly in real space. The pair state |i,d⟩\ket{i,d} [Fig. 5(c)] is constructed explicitly for separations 0≤d≤D0\leq d\leq D, its exact overlap and Hamiltonian matrix elements are evaluated on sparse product states, and the resulting generalized eigen-problem H⁡(q)​ψ=ω​𝒪​(q)​ψH(q)\psi=\omega\,\mathcal{O}(q)\psi is solved at each total momentum by canonical orthogonalization of the nonorthogonal metric. The DSF is obtained from the spectral weight of the d=0d=0 source (Appendix D). The truncation parameter DD is the maximum kink–antikink separation, with D=0D=0 corresponding exactly to the coincident pair, or local triplon. Increasing DD therefore provides a direct way to follow how a locally created S=1S=1 excitation changes as its two spin-1/21/2 constituents are allowed to separate.

The construction is anchored by exact diagonalization (ED) in the reduced Hilbert space. The closed-form spinon dispersions entering the two-kink analysis determine only energy differences, so the single additive constant EKE_{K} is fixed by matching the bottom of the two-spinon continuum to the ED singlet–triplet gap: the gap is computed by sparse Lanczos diagonalization of periodic rings of N=4N=4–1212 unit cells and extrapolated linearly in 1/N1/N to the production size N=32N=32 (Appendix D). ED further serves as an independent benchmark of the DMRG ground states at small system sizes.

III Results

III.1 Ground-state characterization across the dimerized phase

We study the ground state for an OBC system of size L=64L=64 with DMRG at three regimes within the gapped dimerized phase, which occupies 0.49≲r≲1.50.49\lesssim r\lesssim 1.5 [4, 31] and is bounded by two transitions of opposite character. Its lower boundary is a continuous transition into a gapless phase adiabatically connected to the uniform antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chain [4], whose low-energy excitations are the des Cloizeaux-Pearson two-spinon continuum [9, 27]; its upper boundary is a first-order transition into the gapless noncollinear phase studied by  [31]. Our study bridges these two limits, the Heisenberg chain below and the noncollinear phase above, through the exactly solvable VBS at the center: r=0.72r=0.72 probes the approach to the continuous lower edge, r=1.00r=1.00 the exact low entangled VBS, and r=1.38r=1.38 the approach to the first-order upper edge.

Dimer order and entanglement.

Figure 2 characterizes the ground state using two complementary diagnostics of the dimer order: the bond-resolved energy [panels (a)-(c)] and the bipartite entanglement entropy at every bond [panel (d)]. Panels (a)-(c) resolve the energy onto the three inequivalent bonds in the sawtooth triangle. At the VBS point [Fig. 2(b)] the intra-cell apex-base bonds are exact singlets (⟨𝐒⋅𝐒⟩=−34\langle\mathbf{S}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{S}\rangle=-\tfrac{3}{4}) while the apex-to-next-cell and chain bonds carry zero energy: the ground state is a product of decoupled apex-base singlets; consequently the dimer order Cdimer=⟨𝐒iA⋅𝐒i+1B⟩−⟨𝐒iA⋅𝐒iB⟩C_{\rm dimer}=\langle\mathbf{S}^{A}_{i}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{S}^{B}_{i+1}\rangle-\langle\mathbf{S}^{A}_{i}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{S}^{B}_{i}\rangle, attains its maximal value 34\tfrac{3}{4}. The other two points behave differently; at r=1.38r=1.38 [Fig. 2(c)] the strong dimerization survives almost intact (Cdimer=0.73C_{\rm dimer}=0.73), very close to the VBS value although it lies near the upper phase boundary rupper≈1.5r_{\mathrm{upper}}\!\approx\!1.5. This is a direct signature of the first-order phase transition between the dimer phase and the noncollinear phase: rather than slow continuous decay to zero, the order strongly survives right up to the phase boundary and abruptly drops to ∼10−4\sim\!10^{-4} across it  [31]. At r=0.72r=0.72 [Fig. 2(a)] the bond contrast is already substantially reduced (Cdimer=0.34C_{\rm dimer}=0.34) as the apex-to-next-cell bonds strengthen, the growing antiferromagnetic correlations of the uniform zigzag (JA​BJ_{AB}) chain that the small-rr limit approaches, and the dimerization begins to melt, the expected precursor of a continuous transition. In every regime, the pattern is uniform through the bulk, confirming a homogeneously dimerized ground state with open-boundary effects at the edges.

The entanglement entropy tells the same story from a complementary angle. For a cut on bond bb that partitions the chain into left and right blocks, the bipartite von Neumann entanglement entropy  [5] of the ground state is

S(b)=−Tr(ρLlnρL)=−∑αλα2(b)lnλα2(b),S(b)=-\Tr\!\big(\rho_{L}\ln\rho_{L}\big)=-\sum_{\alpha}\lambda_{\alpha}^{2}(b)\,\ln\lambda_{\alpha}^{2}(b), (5)

where ρL=TrR​|Ψ0⟩​⟨Ψ0|\rho_{L}=\Tr_{R}|\Psi_{0}\rangle\langle\Psi_{0}| is the reduced density matrix of the left block and {λα​(b)}\{\lambda_{\alpha}(b)\} are the Schmidt coefficients across the cut (the MPS singular values at bond bb, with ∑αλα2=1\sum_{\alpha}\lambda_{\alpha}^{2}=1), so that S⁡(b)S(b) can be extracted directly off the DMRG MPS state. For a product state, λα=δ1,α\lambda_{\alpha}=\delta_{1,\alpha}; therefore, the entanglement entropy vanishes (S⁡(b)=0S(b)=0) on every inter-cell bond. This is clearly observed for r=1r=1 in Fig. 2(d), confirming that the ground state is an exact tensor product of the individual apex-base singlets, precisely the valence-bond solid. Panels [(a)-(c)] and (d) in Fig. 2 are therefore the dual signatures of the same fact: the singlets are perfect and decoupled through their energies, and the absence of entanglement between them. Away from the dimer point, the two regimes carry finite entanglement with qualitatively different profiles that distinguish the two phase boundaries. At r=1.38r=1.38 the entropy is flat across the bulk, saturating to a low, bond-independent plateau (S≈0.36S\!\approx\!0.36): the state is gapped and obeys the area law [17, 10], consistent with the first-order upper transition, on approach to which the gap drops discontinuously into the gapless noncollinear phase at the boundary itself [31]). At r=0.72r=0.72, by contrast, S⁡(b)S(b) shows a pronounced dome shape peaking at the chain center, the finite-size hallmark of proximity to the continuous lower transition, where the gap closes and correlations become long-ranged, approaching the logarithmic (critical) profile of the uniform antiferromagnetic chain [44, 5]. The flat-versus-domed contrast thus reads directly as first-order (gap-preserving) versus continuous (gap-closing) behavior at the two edges of the dimerized phase.

Static structure factor.

The same physics can be read in momentum space. The sublattice-resolved static (equal-time) structure factor is the Fourier transform of the ground-state spin-spin correlation function,

Sσ​σ​(k)=⟨𝐒0σ⋅𝐒0σ⟩+2​∑d≥1cos⁡(k​d)​⟨𝐒0σ⋅𝐒dσ⟩,σ∈{A,B},S^{\sigma\sigma}(k)=\expectationvalue{\mathbf S^\sigma_0\!\cdot\!\mathbf S^\sigma_0}+2\sum_{d\geq 1}\cos(kd)\,\expectationvalue{\mathbf S^\sigma_0\!\cdot\!\mathbf S^\sigma_{d}},\qquad\sigma\in\{A,B\}, (6)

the position of its maximum is the dominant correlation wavevector, its height and width measure the strength and range of the correlations, and a flat Sσ​σ​(k)S^{\sigma\sigma}(k) signals the absence of any inter-site correlation. Figure 3 shows SA​A​(k)S^{AA}(k) (apex) and SB​B​(k)S^{BB}(k) (basal). At the VBS point, the same sublattice correlations vanish for every d≥1d\geq 1, so Sσ​σ​(k)=⟨𝐒0σ⋅𝐒0σ⟩=34S^{\sigma\sigma}(k)=\expectationvalue{\mathbf S^\sigma_0\!\cdot\!\mathbf S^\sigma_0}=\tfrac{3}{4} is exactly flat, another momentum-space signature of the decoupled-dimer VBS, alongside the bond energies [Fig. 2(a)-(c)] and the vanishing entanglement [Fig. 2(d)]. Away from the dimer point, it sits at k=0k=0 for r=0.72r=0.72 for both apex-apex and basal-basal spins, signifying ferromagnetic-like same sublattice alignment, whereas for r=1.38r=1.38 we observe two different behaviors. The basal channel locks to k=πk=\pi, signifying commensurate staggered antiferromagnetism, whereas the apical channel peaks at an incommensurate wavevector, k≈0.78​πk\approx 0.78\pi, already displaced from π\pi and moving toward k=π/2k=\pi/2. This apical shift is the equilibrium signature of the noncollinear order that sets in beyond the upper transition, whose ordering wavevector approaches k=π/2k=\pi/2 [31].

Taken together, these ground-state diagnostics establish that the three representative couplings probe distinct regimes within the same dimerized phase. The r=0.72r=0.72 state already shows substantial weakening of the dimer order and enhanced entanglement as the continuous lower boundary is approached, whereas the r=1.38r=1.38 state retains strong dimerization while developing incommensurate correlations characteristic of the nearby first-order boundary. With this ground-state evolution across the dimerized phase established, we now turn to the central question of this work: how these distinct regimes are reflected in the dynamical spin response.

III.2 Dynamical structure factor

Figure 4 summarizes the central numerical result of this work: the dynamical structure factor Sz​z​(q,ω)S^{zz}(q,\omega) across the dimerized phase. The left column [(a),(c),(e)] presents the TDVP results over the full extended zone, while the right column [(b),(d),(f)] overlays the analytical and semi-analytical results developed below. Despite the substantial differences in the ground states at the three representative couplings, their dynamical responses share a common qualitative structure. The spectral weight forms a broad continuum dominated by a bright band near its lower edge. The remaining weight spreads into a fainter continuum above it, gathering into a weak secondary maximum in its upper part, with an intensity dip near ω≃JA​B\omega\simeq J_{AB} in between. Qualitatively similar continua have been reported for partially dimerized J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} chains [39].

A natural starting point for understanding the excitation spectrum of a dimerized valence-bond state is the local S=1S=1 triplet excitation of a singlet bond, or triplon. Within the self-consistent bond-operator treatment described in Appendix C, the corresponding one-triplon dispersion for the sawtooth chain is

ωt​(q)=JA​B+JB​B−JA​B2​cos⁡q.\omega_{t}(q)=J_{AB}+\frac{J_{BB}-J_{AB}}{2}\cos q. (7)

At the exact VBS point r=1r=1, this reduces to a flat mode at ωt=JA​B\omega_{t}=J_{AB}, while away from the VBS point the triplon becomes dispersive, with its minimum shifting from q=0q=0 for r<1r<1 to q=πq=\pi for r>1r>1. This conventional triplon picture therefore provides a simple reference for the dynamical response throughout the dimerized phase. Strikingly, however, the TDVP spectra in Fig. 4 are not dominated by this mode, but instead by the broad continua described above.

As described in Sec. II.2, we plot the DSF in the physical (apex-offset) convention over the extended zone q∈[0,4​π]q\in[0,4\pi]. The apical-site offset δA=12\delta_{A}=\tfrac{1}{2} introduces a geometric form factor that makes Sz​z​(q,ω)S^{zz}(q,\omega) asymmetric about q=πq=\pi and symmetric about q=2​πq=2\pi, so that [0,4​π][0,4\pi] is the natural window for comparison with neutron scattering. More remarkably, the spectral weight is suppressed in the vicinity of the expected one-triplon band (red curves in Fig. 4), rather than concentrated around it. This suppression is particularly evident at the exact VBS point, where the flat triplon at ω=JA​B\omega=J_{AB} lies directly in the intensity dip separating the dominant lower band from the faint upper maximum. The persistence of this behavior throughout the dimerized phase suggests that the dominant dynamical excitations are not conventional local triplets. We first describe the numerical spectra across the three representative regimes and then develop their microscopic interpretation in terms of fractionalized kink and antikink excitations.

Exact VBS point (r=1r=1).

At the dimer point [Fig. 4(c),(d)], the spectrum becomes a momentum-independent flat continuum spanning ω≃14​JA​B\omega\simeq\tfrac{1}{4}J_{AB} to 94​JA​B\tfrac{9}{4}J_{AB}. Its intensity is dominated by a flat band near the lower edge and a fainter secondary maximum near ω≃74​JA​B\omega\simeq\tfrac{7}{4}J_{AB}, separated by an intensity dip near ω≃JA​B\omega\simeq J_{AB}. The latter is precisely the energy at which the one-triplon mode is expected.

The one-triplon mode, captured by the self-consistent bond-operator theory [34] (Appendix C) and the MPS-SMA (Appendix B), sits exactly at ωt=JA​B\omega_{t}=J_{AB}. However, in the measured DSF this energy falls in the intensity dip between the dominant lower band and the faint upper maximum; the triplon therefore does not appear as a dominant spectral feature. The numerical MPS-SMA (black points) coincides with this one-triplon line at r=1r=1 for a simple structural reason: acting on a product of on-bond singlets, a local excitation operator SzS^{z} creates an on-bond triplet, so the 2​L2L-dimensional variational space collapses onto the LL single-triplet states, which do not couple across bonds at r=1r=1. The SMA therefore returns the flat triplon at ω=JA​B\omega=J_{AB}, while the TDVP spectrum contains substantial spectral weight both below and above this energy.

Away from the dimer point (r≠1r\neq 1).

For r=0.72r=0.72 and r=1.38r=1.38 [Fig. 4(a),(b) and (e),(f)], the dominant low-energy bands acquire dispersion while retaining the same overall continuum structure seen at the VBS point. At r=0.72r=0.72, the minimum of the bright low-energy band is commensurate, sitting at the zone centers q=0q=0, 2​π2\pi, and 4​π4\pi. This low-energy arc can be viewed as the gapped precursor of the des Cloizeaux–Pearson two-spinon continuum of the uniform (zigzag) Heisenberg chain [9, 27].

By contrast, at r=1.38r=1.38 the low-energy response becomes incommensurate. The dominant intensity develops near q≈1.2​πq\approx 1.2\pi and 2.8​π2.8\pi, with much fainter mirror features near q≈0.83​πq\approx 0.83\pi and 3.17​π3.17\pi. Interestingly, this dynamical incommensurability is already anticipated in the ground state: the apical static structure factor peaks at the incommensurate k≈0.78​πk\approx 0.78\pi [Fig. 3(a)], while the basal channel remains locked near π\pi. We show below that the same sublattice selectivity emerges naturally from the two-spinon description of the dynamical excitations.

The upper part of the spectrum follows the same qualitative pattern in both regimes. The faint secondary maximum remains separated from the dominant low-energy band by an intensity dip near ω≃JA​B\omega\simeq J_{AB}, reproducing the same three-feature structure found at the exact VBS point, but now with finite dispersion. As at the VBS point, the expected one-triplon dispersion (red) does not track any of the prominent features of the measured DSF; instead, the spectral weight in its vicinity remains suppressed. The MPS-SMA modes (black points) plunge below the triplon for r≠1r\neq 1; once the ground state is dressed, the local probes acquire overlap with low-lying excitations, but the resulting branch does not provide a dispersion estimate for any of the prominent bands observed in the DSF.

The common continuum structure across all three regimes therefore calls for a description beyond local triplon excitations. We now show that it arises naturally from deconfined spin-1/21/2 domain walls of the dimerized ground state.

III.3 Spinon origin of the dynamical continuum

To identify the microscopic origin of the continuum, it is useful to begin at the exactly solvable VBS point, where the elementary excitations admit a particularly transparent real-space description. The two degenerate apex–base singlet coverings [Fig. 5(a),(b)] support domain walls carrying spin S=12S=\tfrac{1}{2}, conventionally referred to as kink and antikink spinons. The kink is an orphaned basal spin whose triangle retains its singlet, while the antikink is an orphaned apical spin whose triangle has lost its singlet [Fig. 5(c)]. A local SzS^{z} excitation carries Δ​S=1\Delta S=1 and therefore creates these domain walls in pairs. The corresponding pair state |i,d⟩\ket{i,d} contains a kink k\rm k at cell ii and an antikink k¯\bar{\rm k} at cell i+di+d. Crucially, separating the two domain walls does not produce an energy cost that grows with their separation. The intervening region simply switches from covering I\mathrm{I} to the exactly degenerate covering II\mathrm{II}, leaving the number of intact singlets unchanged at L−1L-1. The diagonal energy is therefore

⟨i,d|⁡(H−E0)​|i,d⟩=34​JA​B+14​JA​B​δd,0,\bra{i,d}(H-E_{0})\ket{i,d}=\tfrac{3}{4}J_{AB}+\tfrac{1}{4}J_{AB}\,\delta_{d,0}, (8)

the dd-independent rest energy of the one dissolved singlet plus a contact term for the on-bond triplet. The pair potential therefore vanishes at every separation, V⁡(d)=0V(d)=011 1 Only singlet bonds contribute to the diagonal because, on a product state, any bond that is not itself a singlet has zero expectation: ⟨𝐒i⋅𝐒j⟩=⟨𝐒i⟩⋅⟨𝐒j⟩=0\expectationvalue{\mb S_i\!\cdot\!\mb S_j}=\expectationvalue{\mb S_i}\!\cdot\!\expectationvalue{\mb S_j}=0, since ⟨𝐒⟩=0\expectationvalue{\mb S}=0 for a spin inside a singlet. In particular, the base-base bonds, which never host a singlet, drop out of the diagonal at every rr, not only at the VBS point. They act only off-diagonally, where they generate the wall hopping at r≠1r\neq 1.. This is analogous to the deconfinement mechanism for the soliton spinons of the Majumdar–Ghosh chain, whose two dimer coverings are also exactly degenerate [40]. It contrasts with confined domain-wall pairs (mesons) bound by a growing potential in quantum spin chains [23, 24, 30] and with two-dimensional valence-bond solids, where a separated pair generally drags a string of disrupted dimers and is confined into a triplon [32, 33].

The spinon picture can be tested against the TDVP spectrum at two complementary levels. First, the single-kink and single-antikink dispersions determine the kinematic support of the two-spinon continuum and can therefore be compared directly with the dispersion observed in Sz​z​(q,ω)S^{zz}(q,\omega). Second, the kinematic boundaries alone do not determine how the spectral weight is distributed within the continuum. We address this separately in Sec. III.4 by constructing the kink–antikink pair explicitly with a finite maximum separation.

Because the kink and antikink are deconfined, their pair energy is additive, and the continuum is given by the cross-convolution of the two spinon bands,

ω⁡(q)=εk​(k1)+εk¯​(q−k1),\omega(q)=\varepsilon_{\rm k}(k_{1})+\varepsilon_{\bar{\rm k}}(q-k_{1}), (9)

with the internal momentum k1k_{1} free (derived in Appendix D). At the VBS point, εk≡0\varepsilon_{\rm k}\equiv 0 and εk¯​(k)=(54+cos⁡k)​JA​B\varepsilon_{\bar{\rm k}}(k)=(\tfrac{5}{4}+\cos k)J_{AB}, so ω⁡(q)=(54+cos⁡(q−k1))​JA​B\omega(q)=(\tfrac{5}{4}+\cos(q-k_1))J_{AB} sweeps the full antikink band [14,94]​JA​B[\tfrac{1}{4},\tfrac{9}{4}]J_{AB} at every qq. The flatness is therefore a direct consequence of the dispersionless kink: it absorbs the total momentum at zero energy cost and frees the antikink to sit anywhere in its band, so the antikink bandwidth survives as the full width 2​JA​B2J_{AB} of a momentum-independent continuum.

This closed-form continuum is precisely what is observed numerically. Its lower edge, flat at ω=14​JA​B\omega=\tfrac{1}{4}J_{AB}, runs through the dominant bright band of the measured DSF [thick green line in Fig. 4(d)], identifying the dominant low-energy feature as the lower edge of the two-spinon continuum. The upper edge at 94​JA​B\tfrac{9}{4}J_{AB} bounds the visible weight from above, while the faint secondary maximum at ω≃74​JA​B\omega\simeq\tfrac{7}{4}J_{AB} lies within the same continuum. Thus the dominant lower band, the faint upper maximum, and the dip between them all lie within the kinematic band [14,94]​JA​B[\tfrac{1}{4},\tfrac{9}{4}]J_{AB}. In particular, the one-triplon energy ω=JA​B\omega=J_{AB} lies inside the continuum rather than defining a distinct excitation branch.

Away from the exact VBS point, the base-base bonds turn on hopping of the domain walls, and both spinons acquire dispersion. The resulting closed-form dispersions (Appendix D) are

εk​(k)\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\rm k}(k) =EK−(JB​B−JA​B)​4+5​cos⁡k5+4​cos⁡k,\displaystyle=E_{K}-(J_{BB}-J_{AB})\,\frac{4+5\cos k}{5+4\cos k}, (10)
εk¯​(k)\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\bar{\rm k}}(k) =εk​(k)+12​JB​B​(1+2​cos⁡k),\displaystyle=\varepsilon_{\rm k}(k)+\tfrac{1}{2}J_{BB}\,(1+2\cos k), (11)

where the additive constant EKE_{K} is fixed by the exact-diagonalization spectral gap (Appendix D), an anchor that at r=1r=1 recovers the expected value ≃0.21​JA​B\simeq 0.21J_{AB} [28]. At r=1r=1, Eqs. (10) and (11) reduce to the dimer limit εk=0\varepsilon_{\rm k}=0 and εk¯=(54+cos⁡k)​JA​B\varepsilon_{\bar{\rm k}}=(\tfrac{5}{4}+\cos k)J_{AB}.

Inserting Eqs. (10) and (11) into the convolution (9) generates the two-spinon continua for r=0.72r=0.72 and r=1.38r=1.38 [Fig. 4(b),(f)]. The central observation at the dimer point carries over throughout the dimerized phase: the lower edge of the two-spinon continuum (thick green) traces the dominant low-energy band of the measured DSF. As rr changes, the minima of these bands migrate across the zone, and the closed-form continuum edge reproduces this migration.

At r=0.72r=0.72, the minimum remains commensurate, sitting at the zone centers q=0q=0, 2​π2\pi, and 4​π4\pi. Although the low-energy arc is the gapped precursor of the des Cloizeaux–Pearson two-spinon continuum of the uniform Heisenberg chain [9, 27], quantitatively its shape is still described by the kink–antikink edge of Eqs. (10) and (11), as seen in Fig. 4(b).

By contrast, at r=1.38r=1.38 the band minimum is incommensurate, and its position follows directly from the spinon dispersions. The kink band is stationary only at k=0k=0 and k=πk=\pi, so the incommensurability is carried entirely by the antikink. The curvature of Eq. (11) at k=πk=\pi is 9​JA​B−8​JB​B9J_{AB}-8J_{BB}, which changes sign at r=98r=\tfrac{9}{8}. For 1≤r≤981\leq r\leq\tfrac{9}{8}, the antikink minimum is locked to the commensurate point k=πk=\pi, while for r>98r>\tfrac{9}{8} it moves continuously according to

cos⁡k∗=3​1−1/r−54.\cos k^{*}=\frac{3\sqrt{1-1/r}-5}{4}. (12)

At r=1.38r=1.38, k∗=0.827​πk^{*}=0.827\pi, together with its reflection 2​π−k∗=1.173​π2\pi-k^{*}=1.173\pi, giving an exactly degenerate pair of minima flanking q=πq=\pi, with q=πq=\pi itself a shallow local maximum between them (≲0.01​JA​B\lesssim 0.01J_{AB} throughout the phase). In the extended zone q∈[0,4​π]q\in[0,4\pi], this produces four minima q=2​π​n±k∗q=2\pi n\pm k^{*} [Fig. 4(f)]. The two minima on either side of q=πq=\pi (and their mirrors about q=3​πq=3\pi) are not equivalent in intensity: the apex form factor 12​(1−cos⁡q2)\tfrac{1}{2}(1-\cos\tfrac{q}{2}) favors the one closer to q=2​πq=2\pi. We therefore observe brighter intensity in the DSF near q≈1.2​πq\approx 1.2\pi and 2.8​π2.8\pi [Fig. 4(e),(f)], while the mirror partners near q≈0.83​πq\approx 0.83\pi and 3.17​π3.17\pi remain faint. This also explains the sublattice selectivity noted above: the antikink, which is the apical domain wall, carries the incommensurability, while the kink, which is the basal domain wall, remains commensurate.

The same kinematics organizes the upper part of the spectrum. In both regimes, the faint secondary maximum lies inside the continuum, below the upper edge that bounds the visible weight, with the intensity dip near ω≃JA​B\omega\simeq J_{AB} between it and the dominant band. The closed-form spinon dispersions therefore determine where the continuum lies in momentum and energy. To understand why the spectral weight is distributed within it as observed in TDVP, we now turn to an explicit real-space construction of the kink–antikink pair.

III.4 Spectral weight and triplon fractionalization

The closed-form spinon dispersions determine the kinematic support of the continuum and account for the location of its dominant low-energy edge, but they do not determine how the spectral weight is distributed within it. To address this question, we employ the finite-DD two-kink construction of Sec. II.4, which follows a locally created S=1S=1 excitation as its two spin-1/21/2 constituents are allowed to separate up to a maximum distance DD.

Figure 6 shows this reconstruction. At D=0D=0, the spectrum consists of the single triplon band, flat at ω=JA​B\omega=J_{AB} for r=1r=1 and dispersing for r≠1r\neq 1 [Fig. 6(a),(e),(i)]. As DD increases, the pair delocalizes, and the local S=1S=1 spin flip fractionalizes into a pair of S=12S=\tfrac{1}{2} constituents. The single band splits into D+1D+1 bands and progressively redistributes its spectral weight toward the lower two-spinon edge. Already at D=6D=6, the discrete bands densify toward a continuum whose brightest weight lies well below ω=JA​B\omega=J_{AB} [Fig. 6(c),(g),(k)].

Overlaying the D=6D=6 bands on the numerical DSF [Fig. 6(d),(h),(l)] shows agreement both in the band positions and in the relative distribution of spectral weight. The reconstruction reproduces the dominant lower band, the faint upper maximum, and the intensity dip near ω≃JA​B\omega\simeq J_{AB} in all three regimes. In particular, the fainter upper-intensity maxima are not separate excitations; their shapes and positions coincide with upper two-kink bands. At r=1r=1, the flat feature near ω≃1.7​JA​B\omega\simeq 1.7\,J_{AB} matches the D=6D=6 band at 1.71​JA​B1.71\,J_{AB}. At r=1.38r=1.38, the brightest upper feature (ω≃1.45​JA​B\omega\simeq 1.45\,J_{AB} at q=2​πq=2\pi) lies on the D=6D=6 band at 1.43​JA​B1.43\,J_{AB}, while at r=0.72r=0.72 the brightest upper feature (ω≃1.80​JA​B\omega\simeq 1.80\,J_{AB} at q=2​πq=2\pi) is traced by a D=6D=6 band at 1.87​JA​B1.87\,J_{AB}. Thus the closed-form convolution determines where the continuum lies [Fig. 4, green], while the finite-DD two-kink construction explains how the spectral weight is distributed within it [Fig. 6]. Together, they show that the full low-energy lineshape of the DSF is generated by the deconfined kink–antikink pair.

The finite-DD construction also makes explicit why the bond-operator triplon, which can be quantitatively successful in two-dimensional valence-bond solids, traces no prominent feature of the sawtooth spectrum. The triplon is the D=0D=0 limit of the two-kink state [Fig. 6(a),(e),(i)], and restricting the excitation to D=0D=0 is justified only when a confining potential keeps the pair bound. In two dimensions, a separated pair generally drags a string of disrupted dimers, causing V⁡(d)V(d) to grow with separation [32, 33, 38]; deconfined spinons instead require a different ground state, such as a quantum spin liquid [15]. The resulting confined S=1S=1 quasiparticles are observed, for example, in the pinwheel valence-bond solid of two-dimensional kagome antiferromagnets, where triplon bands form the primary excitations and are quantitatively described by dimer-based theories, with continuum scattering appearing only above a higher-energy threshold [26, 25, 46, 6].

On the sawtooth chain, by contrast, V⁡(d)=0V(d)=0 [Eq. (8)], and as DD grows the spectral weight drains from the local triplon into the continuum [Fig. 6], leaving an intensity dip near ω≃JA​B\omega\simeq J_{AB} where the sharpest triplon feature would be expected in a confined system. The spinon dispersions and finite-DD reconstruction therefore provide complementary evidence for the same physical picture: the former determine where the two-spinon continuum lies in momentum and energy, while the latter shows how the spectral weight of a locally created triplet is transferred into that continuum as the kink and antikink are allowed to separate. Together with the TDVP results, this identifies the broad dynamical response throughout the dimerized phase as the spectral signature of spinon fractionalization.

IV Summary and outlook

We have computed the ground-state properties and the zero-temperature dynamical structure factor of the dimerized phase of the antiferromagnetic sawtooth chain at three representative points, r=0.72r=0.72, 1.001.00, and 1.381.38. We employ a U⁡(1)U(1)-symmetric DMRG ++ TDVP pipeline, benchmarked against the exactly solvable valence-bond solid at r=1r=1 and exact diagonalization. The bond-resolved dimer order, bipartite entanglement entropy, and sublattice-resolved static structure factor consistently characterize a dimerized phase bounded by transitions of opposite character. Approaching the continuous lower boundary, the dimer order weakens, and the entanglement grows, whereas toward the first-order upper boundary the strong dimerization persists while the apical correlations become incommensurate, anticipating the noncollinear phase beyond.

The dynamical structure factor exhibits a broad continuum throughout the dimerized phase: a dominant lower band carries the largest share of the spectral weight, while the remaining weight spreads into a much fainter continuum with a weak secondary maximum in its upper part. Remarkably, the spectral weight is suppressed in the vicinity of the expected one-triplon band rather than concentrated around it. Our central result is the identification of this response with a deconfined two-spinon continuum built from the kink and antikink domain walls between the two degenerate singlet coverings: a locally created Δ​S=1\Delta S=1 excitation fractionalizes into two S=1/2S=1/2 constituents. This assignment is supported by two complementary calculations. The spinon dispersions determine the kinematic boundaries of the continuum and track its prominent low-energy edge, including the incommensurate minima observed at r=1.38r=1.38, while the finite-DD projected two-spinon calculation reproduces the redistribution of spectral weight into the continuum, including the intensity dip near the expected triplon band and the fainter upper maximum. The dimerized phase thus connects, in both its static correlations and dynamical response, the physics of the des Cloizeaux–Pearson two-spinon continuum of the uniform Heisenberg chain on one side and the gapless noncollinear phase on the other [31], with the exactly solvable VBS point providing a particularly transparent realization of the underlying spinon physics.

Two directions follow naturally. First, the sawtooth chain provides a useful building block for understanding the recently discovered class of Ti3+ kagome fluorides, where strong modulations of the exchange interactions generate coupled sawtooth-like motifs [42, 43]. Broad magnetic continua have also been observed in the dynamical response of these materials, including Cs8LiNa3Ti12F48 [43]. The real materials, however, are two-dimensional, and their excitation spectra necessarily involve couplings between the sawtooth motifs as well as other details absent from the present one-dimensional model. An important question for future work is therefore how the deconfined spinons identified here evolve upon coupling the chains into two dimensions, and in particular whether and how inter-chain interactions confine, or weakly confine, the kink-antikink pairs into bound excitations. Second, the domain-wall picture developed here should provide a useful starting point for studying the excitations at finite magnetic field, where flat-band physics is closely connected to localized-magnon states and the magnetization plateaus and jumps of the sawtooth family [36, 8]. We leave these questions to future work.

DMRG convergence and ground-state accuracy.

In Table 1 we present the convergence record of the six production ground states (L=32L=32 for seeding the dynamics, L=64L=64 for the equilibrium characterization). The largest bond dimension was reached in all r≠1r\neq 1 cases, signifying the presence of truncation errors, the number of sweeps to convergence (sweeping continues until the energy per site is stable to the tolerance of 10−710^{-7} over a sliding window of ten half-sweeps), and the energy variance per site,

v≡⟨H2⟩−⟨H⟩2N​JA​B2,v\;\equiv\;\frac{\langle H^{2}\rangle-\langle H\rangle^{2}}{N\,J_{AB}^{2}}, (14)

contracted exactly as a two-MPO-layer sandwich on the converged MPS (v=0v=0 for an exact eigenstate). A fixed bond dimension can bias DMRG toward metastable solutions; the sweep histories provide a direct check [Fig. 7(a)]. r=1.38r=1.38 is the most difficult case of convergence among all three values of rr considered. At r=1.38r=1.38, L=64L=64, the energy passes through an intermediate plateau before falling onto the true ground state, after which it is stable to ∼3×10−11\sim 3\times 10^{-11} per site for the next ten half sweeps concluding the simulation. The other two rr follow a similar pattern but are converged at a lesser number of sweeps with a few orders of magnitude smaller vv. The exactly solvable case of r=1r=1 is reproduced by DMRG with a bond dimension of 4, thus implying the tensor product VBS state.

TDVP error control.

The real-time evolution uses the two-site TDVP integrator, so the bond dimension grows adaptively with the entanglement of |ϕσ​(t)⟩|\phi^{\sigma}(t)\rangle up to χTDVP=600\chi_{\rm TDVP}=600. The error is monitored through the per-step truncated weight εstep​(t)\varepsilon_{\rm step}(t), the summed discarded Schmidt weight of all two-site updates within a single time step [Fig. 7(b)]. It rises steeply during the initial entanglement growth of the propagating excitation, saturates once the bond dimension reaches its cap. At tfinal=8​JA​B−1t_{\rm final}=8\,J_{AB}^{-1}, εstep≃O⁡(10−5)\varepsilon_{\rm step}\simeq O(10^{-5}) at r=1r=1, and ≃O⁡(10−4)\simeq O(10^{-4}) at r≠1r\neq 1 (the two values per regime are the two source channels). As an end-to-end convergence test in the least favorable regime, the entire pipeline was repeated at r=1.38r=1.38 with χTDVP=480\chi_{\rm TDVP}=480 to compute the relative error in the DSF. The resulting Sz​z​(q,ω)S^{zz}(q,\omega) differs from the χTDVP=600\chi_{\rm TDVP}=600 result by 0.6%0.6\% in relative L2L^{2} norm, with a maximum pointwise deviation of 0.7%0.7\% of the peak intensity, i.e. the DSF maps shown in the main text are converged in χ\chi on the scale of the plots (Fig. 8).

Appendix B Single-mode approximation

Variational framework.

For a set of local excitation operators {Ωjσ}\{\Omega^{\sigma}_{j}\} acting on a ground state |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle (energy E0E_{0}), the trial states Ωjσ​|Ψ0⟩\Omega^{\sigma}_{j}|\Psi_{0}\rangle are generally non-orthogonal, so the variational spectrum follows from the generalized eigen-problem [Eq. (4) of the main text]

H~​ψ\displaystyle\tilde{H}\,\psi =ω​𝒪​ψ,\displaystyle=\omega\,\mathcal{O}\,\psi, (15)
𝒪i​jσ​σ′\displaystyle\mathcal{O}^{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}_{ij} =⟨Ψ0|(Ωiσ)†​Ωjσ′|Ψ0⟩,\displaystyle=\langle\Psi_{0}|(\Omega^{\sigma}_{i})^{\dagger}\Omega^{\sigma^{\prime}}_{j}|\Psi_{0}\rangle, (16)
H~i​jσ​σ′\displaystyle\tilde{H}^{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}_{ij} =⟨Ψ0|(Ωiσ)†​(H−E0)​Ωjσ′|Ψ0⟩.\displaystyle=\langle\Psi_{0}|(\Omega^{\sigma}_{i})^{\dagger}(H-E_{0})\Omega^{\sigma^{\prime}}_{j}|\Psi_{0}\rangle. (17)

Equation (15) is the stationarity condition of the Rayleigh–Ritz principle restricted to the trial subspace: extremizing R⁡(ψ)=ψ†​H~​ψ/ψ†​𝒪​ψR(\psi)=\psi^{\dagger}\tilde{H}\psi/\psi^{\dagger}\mathcal{O}\psi over the coefficients yields Eq. (15) with ω=R⁡(ψ)\omega=R(\psi), the metric 𝒪\mathcal{O} being the non-orthogonality of the trial states. The trial subspace is a subspace of the full Hilbert space, each generalized eigenvalue is a variational upper bound on the true excitation of the same rank. For a single operator this collapses to the single-mode Rayleigh quotient  [39]. The multi-operator (matrix) form used here lets a small set of local probes mix variationally.

One-bond triplon branch.

The SzS^{z}, Δ​Stotz=0\Delta S^{z}_{\rm tot}=0 singlet-to-triplet operator on the apex–base bond, Ωjmag=SBjz−SAjz\Omega^{\rm mag}_{j}=S^{z}_{B_{j}}-S^{z}_{A_{j}}, gives to one-bond order

ωmag​(k)=JA​B+JB​B−JA​B2​cos⁡k,\omega_{\rm mag}(k)=J_{AB}+\tfrac{J_{BB}-J_{AB}}{2}\cos k, (18)

flat at ω=JA​B\omega=J_{AB} at the VBS point r=1r=1, with band minimum migrating from k=0k=0 (r<1r<1) to k=πk=\pi (r>1r>1). This is the SMA realization of the single-triplet mode and coincides with the self-consistent bond-operator triplon of Appendix C; the two analytic routes agree across the dimerized phase. Within the numerical basis {SBjz,SAjz}\{S^{z}_{B_{j}},S^{z}_{A_{j}}\} used below, this triplon is the antisymmetric combination SBjz−SAjzS^{z}_{B_{j}}-S^{z}_{A_{j}}; the symmetric combination SBjz+SAjzS^{z}_{B_{j}}+S^{z}_{A_{j}} builds the total SzS^{z} and annihilates the singlet ground state, a spurious null mode removed below.

Numerical (MPS) SMA.

Beyond the analytic one-bond estimate, we evaluate Eq. (15) numerically on the DMRG ground state, with the trial space spanned by the two one-site probes per cell, {ΩjB=SBjz,ΩjA=SAjz}j=1L\{\Omega^{B}_{j}=S^{z}_{B_{j}},\,\Omega^{A}_{j}=S^{z}_{A_{j}}\}_{j=1}^{L} (2​L2L states). The procedure is as follows:

  1. 1.

    Matrix elements. Explicitly build the 2​L×2​L2L\times 2L matrices 𝒪i​jσ​σ′\mathcal{O}^{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}_{ij} and H~i​jσ​σ′\tilde{H}^{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}_{ij} as MPS-MPO-MPS sandwhiches, ⟨Ψ0|(Ωiσ)†​O^​Ωjσ′|Ψ0⟩\langle\Psi_{0}|(\Omega^{\sigma}_{i})^{\dagger}\,\hat{O}\,\Omega^{\sigma^{\prime}}_{j}|\Psi_{0}\rangle with O^∈{𝟙,H}\hat{O}\in\{\mathbbm{1},H\}.

  2. 2.

    Generalized solve. After Hermitian symmetrization, the near-singular metric is regularized by a small diagonal shift 𝒪→𝒪+ε​ 1\mathcal{O}\to\mathcal{O}+\varepsilon\,\mathbbm{1} (ε=10−10\varepsilon=10^{-10}) and the positive-definite generalized symmetric eigen-problem is solved with LAPACK hegvd (internally a Cholesky of 𝒪+ε​𝟙\mathcal{O}+\varepsilon\mathbbm{1}).

  3. 3.

    Momentum projection. Each eigenvector is projected onto the cell-momentum plane waves |k,σ⟩=L−1/2∑je−i​k​jΩjσ|Ψ0⟩|k,\sigma\rangle=L^{-1/2}\sum_{j}e^{-ikj}\,\Omega^{\sigma}_{j}|\Psi_{0}\rangle on the grid k=2​π​m/Lk=2\pi m/L; its effective momentum is the kk of maximal weight.

  4. 4.

    Null-mode filtering. On the singlet ground state ∑j(SBjz+SAjz)​|Ψ0⟩=Stotz​|Ψ0⟩=0\sum_{j}(S^{z}_{B_{j}}+S^{z}_{A_{j}})|\Psi_{0}\rangle=S^{z}_{\rm tot}|\Psi_{0}\rangle=0, producing a spurious ω≈0\omega\!\approx\!0 eigenvalue—a Goldstone of the U⁡(1)U(1) total-SzS^{z} conservation, not a physical excitation; eigenvalues with |ω|<10−3|\omega|<10^{-3} are discarded.

The lowest non-null eigenvalue at each kk is the variational SMA dispersion. Validation: at the exact VBS (r=1r=1) the method returns the flat triplon at ω=JA​B\omega=J_{AB}, reproducing Eq. (18).

Interpretation of the lowest branch.

At the exact VBS point the ground state is a tensor product of on-bond singlets, on which a local SzS^{z} creates only the on-bond triplet. The kink and antikink are non-local domain walls, invisible to any one-site operator, so the MPS-SMA necessarily returns the flat triplon at ω=JA​B\omega=J_{AB}, coinciding with the one-bond result (18). Away from the VBS point, the dressed ground state lets the same local probes overlap with the much lower kink-antikink pair continuum, and the lowest branch plunges below the triplon. The lowest MPS-SMA branch is therefore a loose variational upper bound on the two-spinon continuum, not a triplon estimate. The agreement with the triplon at r=1r=1 reflects the operator redundancy of the exact VBS, not a triplon character of the low-energy spectrum.

Appendix D Kink–antikink (two-spinon) theory of the low-energy continuum

The prominent low-energy feature of the DSF is not the triplon of Appendix C but a two-spinon continuum built from the two degenerate valence-bond-solid (VBS) coverings. We give the construction in full, following the dressed-domain-wall approach [16]. It is the deconfined counterpart of the two-kink meson problem [24]: a constrained two-wall Hilbert space carrying a non-orthogonal metric, an effective hopping Hamiltonian.

D.1 Domain walls and the non-orthogonal metric

At r=1r=1 the exact ground state is a product of apex–base singlets on one of two coverings |I⟩,|II⟩\ket{\mathrm{I}},\ket{\mathrm{II}}. Its elementary excitations are the two domain walls between them: a kink (an orphaned basal spin, whose triangle still carries a singlet, so it costs no energy and is dispersionless) and an antikink (an orphaned apical spin, whose triangle loses its singlet, costing 34​JA​B\tfrac{3}{4}J_{AB}). A single wall is a product state that differs from a partner displaced by dd cells only on the 2​d+12d{+}1 sites separating the two orphan positions; elsewhere the two coverings coincide and overlap unity. On this “domino” the two coverings pair the intervening spins into staggered singlets, and the free end fixes a unique alternating spin string, each mismatched singlet contributing a factor −12-\tfrac{1}{2}. The overlap is therefore a geometric cascade,

o⁡(d)\displaystyle o(d) ≡⟨wall|wall+d⟩=(−12)|d|,\displaystyle\equiv\innerproduct{\text{wall}}{\text{wall}+d}=\quantity(-\tfrac 12)^{|d|}, (35)
o⁡(k)\displaystyle o(k) =∑do⁡(d)​ei​k​d=35+4​cos⁡k,\displaystyle=\sum_{d}o(d)\,e^{ikd}=\frac{3}{5+4\cos k},

computable in O⁡(d)O(d) time (a transfer matrix along the domino, not a sum over 2d2^{d} spin configurations). The domain-wall basis is thus non-orthogonal and carries the metric o⁡(k)o(k) (peaked at k=πk=\pi, o=3o=3; minimal at k=0k=0, o=13o=\tfrac{1}{3}). For a two-wall state, the overlap factorizes into the two independent domino chains, up to a local correction where the walls share a triangle.

D.2 Effective two-wall Hamiltonian

The Hamiltonian in Eq. (1) is a sum of nearest-neighbor bonds, and any two two-wall states share an identical singlet background away from the walls; every matrix element ⟨i,d|⁡(H,𝟙)​|i′,d′⟩\bra{i,d}(H,\mathbbm{1})\ket{i', d'} is fixed by a bounded neighborhood of the walls which is independent of system size.

Diagonal (V⁡(d)=0V(d)=0).

Each intact apex-base singlet contributes −34​JA​B-\tfrac{3}{4}J_{AB} (L−1L{-}1 of them, independent of dd). Every base-base JB​BJ_{BB} bond connects different singlets, so ⟨𝐒⋅𝐒⟩=⟨𝐒⟩⋅⟨𝐒⟩=0\expectationvalue{\mathbf S\!\cdot\!\mathbf S}=\expectationvalue{\mathbf S}\!\cdot\!\expectationvalue{\mathbf S}=0. The base-base coupling is inert on the diagonal at every rr, and at d=0d=0 the collapsed triangle carries a triplet contributing 14​JA​B\tfrac{1}{4}J_{AB}. Relative to the VBS energy E0=−34​L​JA​BE_{0}=-\tfrac{3}{4}LJ_{AB}, this reproduces Eq. (8) of the main text, the pair potential vanishes at every separation, V⁡(d)=0V(d)=0 for d≥1d\geq 1.

Hopping.

The off-diagonal elements come from the exchange 12(Si+Sj−+h.c.)\tfrac{1}{2}(S^{+}_{i}S^{-}_{j}+\mathrm{h.c.}) acting on a bond that touches an orphan, which displaces one wall by a single cell. Each amplitude is a finite-cluster matrix element (for example, the intra-domino base–base bond that hops the kink by one cell has bare matrix element −38-\tfrac{3}{8}, evaluated below).

Assembly.

With a flat diagonal [Eq. (8)] and finite hoppings, an eigenstate |ψ⟩=∑i,dψ⁡(i,d)​|i,d⟩\ket{\psi}=\sum_{i,d}\psi(i,d)\ket{i,d} obeys the real-space generalized eigen-problem (H−E0)​ψ=ω​𝒪​ψ(H-E_{0})\psi=\omega\,\mathcal{O}\psi, the non-orthogonal metric 𝒪\mathcal{O} [Eq. (35)] sitting on the right-hand side. This is the sawtooth analogue of the effective two-kink Hamiltonian of Ref. [24], with V⁡(d)=0V(d)=0 in place of their confining potential and 𝒪≠𝟙\mathcal{O}\neq\mathbbm{1} from the domino overlaps.

D.3 Single-spinon dispersions in closed form

For arbitrary rr, split the Hamiltonian as H=Hr=1+VH=H_{r=1}+V, where Hr=1−E0=3​JA​B2​∑lP3/2(l)H_{r=1}-E_{0}=\tfrac{3J_{AB}}{2}\sum_{l}P^{(l)}_{3/2} is the projector sum of the dimer point and V=(JB​B−JA​B)​∑l𝐒bl⋅𝐒bl+1V=(J_{BB}-J_{AB})\sum_{l}\mathbf{S}_{b_{l}}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{S}_{b_{l+1}} collects the base-base deviation. The wall states are the same product states at every rr (they are trial states), so the dispersions of both walls, Eqs. (10)-(11), follow for all rr at once from a handful of finite-cluster matrix elements and one lattice sum. The dimer point is recovered at the end as the V→0V\to 0 special case, and the additive constant EKE_{K} is fixed by the exact-diagonalization (ED) spectral gap.

Kink.

Every triangle of a kink state stays in the spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} sector, so the projector sum annihilates it at every rr and the kink matrix element is carried by VV alone,

h~k​(d)≡⟨ki|⁡(H−E0)​|ki+d⟩=(JB​B−JA​B)​∑l⟨ki|​𝐒bl⋅𝐒bl+1​|ki+d⟩.\begin{split}\tilde{h}_{\rm k}(d)&\equiv\bra{{\rm k}_i}(H-E_{0})\ket{{\rm k}_{i+d}}\\ &=(J_{BB}-J_{AB})\sum_{l}\bra{{\rm k}_i}\mathbf{S}_{b_{l}}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{S}_{b_{l+1}}\ket{{\rm k}_{i+d}}.\end{split} (36)

At d=0d=0 this vanishes, since the base-base bonds are diagonally inert [Eq. (8)]. The kink’s diagonal energy is JB​BJ_{BB}-independent at every rr, and its dispersion lives entirely off the diagonal. At d=1d=1 the bra and ket differ only on the three-site base–apex–base domino (bi,ai,bi+1)(b_{i},a_{i},b_{i+1}). Any bond with one end outside the domino factorizes through a spectator singlet common to bra and ket, ⟨𝐒⟩singlet=0\expectationvalue{\mathbf S}_{\rm singlet}=0, so only the single internal base–base bond (bi,bi+1)(b_{i},b_{i+1}) survives. Contracting 𝐒bi⋅𝐒bi+1=SbizSbi+1z+12(Sbi+Sbi+1−+h.c.)\mathbf{S}_{b_{i}}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{S}_{b_{i+1}}=S^{z}_{b_{i}}S^{z}_{b_{i+1}}+\tfrac{1}{2}(S^{+}_{b_{i}}S^{-}_{b_{i+1}}+\mathrm{h.c.}) between |sbi​ai⟩​|↑bi+1⟩\ket{s_{b_ia_i}}\!\ket{\uparrow_{b_{i+1}}} and ⟨↑bi|​⟨sai​bi+1|\bra{\uparrow_{b_i}}\!\bra{s_{a_ib_{i+1}}} gives −14−18=−38-\tfrac{1}{4}-\tfrac{1}{8}=-\tfrac{3}{8}, so h~k​(1)=−38​(JB​B−JA​B)\tilde{h}_{\rm k}(1)=-\tfrac{3}{8}\,(J_{BB}-J_{AB}). For general separation the domino holds |d||d| internal base–base bonds, the edge bonds still vanish, and by translation invariance within the domino each internal bond contributes the same increment relative to the overlap o⁡(d)o(d); together with the extensive singlet-sea energy, the matrix element therefore has the exact structure

h⁡(d)=Ebulk​o​(d)+εdom​|d|​o​(d)+hconn​(d),h(d)=E_{\rm bulk}\,o(d)+\varepsilon_{\rm dom}\,|d|\,o(d)+h_{\rm conn}(d), (37)

with Ebulk∝LE_{\rm bulk}\propto L the singlet-sea energy, εdom\varepsilon_{\rm dom} the per-cell domain increment, and hconnh_{\rm conn} a short-range connected part (hconn=0h_{\rm conn}=0 for the kink). The bulk-subtracted ratio

R⁡(d)≡h⁡(d)o⁡(d)−h⁡(0)o⁡(0)R(d)\equiv\frac{h(d)}{o(d)}-\frac{h(0)}{o(0)} (38)

removes EbulkE_{\rm bulk} exactly and is exactly linear in |d||d|; the d=1d=1 element fixes the slope,

Rk​(d)=εdom​|d|,εdom=h~k​(1)o⁡(1)=34​(JB​B−JA​B).R_{\rm k}(d)=\varepsilon_{\rm dom}\,|d|,\qquad\varepsilon_{\rm dom}=\frac{\tilde{h}_{\rm k}(1)}{o(1)}=\tfrac{3}{4}\,(J_{BB}-J_{AB}). (39)

(Diagonalizing finite windows directly instead mixes EbulkE_{\rm bulk} into the extracted bandwidth, which then drifts with window size. Eq. (38) is the window-free object. The linear form and the coefficients are confirmed in exact rational arithmetic against finite-cluster matrix elements on windows of 1010 and 1212 cells.)

Antikink.

The antikink differs in two ways. First, its wall triangle carries spin-32\tfrac{3}{2} weight 12\tfrac{1}{2}, so the projector survives on the diagonal and contributes 34​JA​B​δd,0\tfrac{3}{4}J_{AB}\,\delta_{d,0}, the dissolved singlet of Eq. (8), while VV remains diagonally inert. Second, its domino is apex-base-apex, (ai,bi+1,ai+1)(a_{i},b_{i+1},a_{i+1}), with no internal base-base bond. The VV part vanishes at d=1d=1, and a domain of width dd holds only d−1d-1 internal bonds, so the ramp is εdom​(d−1)\varepsilon_{\rm dom}(d-1). Hence

Rk¯​(d)=εdom​(d−1)−34​JA​B=εdom|d|+C,C=−34​JB​B,\begin{split}R_{\overline{\rm k}}(d)&=\varepsilon_{\rm dom}\,(d-1)-\tfrac{3}{4}J_{AB}\\ &=\varepsilon_{\rm dom}\,|d|+C,\qquad C=-\tfrac{3}{4}J_{BB},\end{split} (40)

the constant combining the dissolved singlet (−34​JA​B-\tfrac{3}{4}J_{AB}) and the one missing internal bond (−εdom-\varepsilon_{\rm dom}), both walls disperse with the same slope.

Fourier transform.

By Eq. (38) the matrix element factors as h⁡(d)=o⁡(d)​[Eref+R⁡(d)]h(d)=o(d)\,[E_{\rm ref}+R(d)] with Eref=h⁡(0)/o⁡(0)E_{\rm ref}=h(0)/o(0) a dd-independent constant, so the single-wall Rayleigh quotient reads

ε⁡(k)=h⁡(k)o⁡(k)=Eref+1o⁡(k)​∑dR⁡(d)​o​(d)​ei​k​d.\varepsilon(k)=\frac{h(k)}{o(k)}=E_{\rm ref}+\frac{1}{o(k)}\sum_{d}R(d)\,o(d)\,e^{ikd}. (41)

The linear ramp reduces everything to a single lattice sum, evaluated with the generating function oz​(k)=∑dz|d|​ei​k​d=(1−z2)/(1−2​z​cos⁡k+z2)o_{z}(k)=\sum_{d}z^{|d|}e^{ikd}=(1-z^{2})/(1-2z\cos k+z^{2}) [which reproduces Eq. (35) at z=−12z=-\tfrac{1}{2}] and z​∂zz|d|=|d|​z|d|z\,\partial_{z}z^{|d|}=|d|\,z^{|d|}:

S⁡(k)≡∑d|d|​(−12)|d|​ei​k​d=z​∂zoz​(k)|z=−12=−4​(4+5​cos⁡k)(5+4​cos⁡k)2,\begin{split}S(k)&\equiv\sum_{d}|d|\,\quantity(-\tfrac 12)^{|d|}e^{ikd}=z\,\partial_{z}o_{z}(k)\Big|_{z=-\frac{1}{2}}\\ &=-\frac{4\,(4+5\cos k)}{(5+4\cos k)^{2}},\end{split} (42)

so that S(k)/o(k)=−43(4+5cosk)/(5+4cosk)S(k)/o(k)=-\tfrac{4}{3}\,(4+5\cos k)/(5+4\cos k). For the kink, ∑dRk​(d)​o​(d)​ei​k​d=εdom​S​(k)\sum_{d}R_{\rm k}(d)\,o(d)\,e^{ikd}=\varepsilon_{\rm dom}S(k), and the prefactors combine as 34×43=1\tfrac{3}{4}\times\tfrac{4}{3}=1. The quotient is exactly Eq. (10), with the additive constant EKE_{K} standing in for the bare reference ErefE_{\rm ref} (anchored below). For the antikink, the extra constant in Eq. (40) adds C​∑d≠0o⁡(d)​ei​k​d=C⁡[o⁡(k)−1]C\sum_{d\neq 0}o(d)\,e^{ikd}=C\,[o(k)-1] to the sum [R⁡(0)=0R(0)=0 by construction], i.e. C⁡[1−1/o⁡(k)]=(−34​JB​B)×[−13​(2+4​cos​k)]=12​JB​B​(1+2​cos​k)C\,[1-1/o(k)]=(-\tfrac{3}{4}J_{BB})\times[-\tfrac{1}{3}(2+4\cos k)]=\tfrac{1}{2}J_{BB}\,(1+2\cos k) to the quotient, exactly the offset of Eq. (11). Since (4+5​cos⁡k)/(5+4​cos⁡k)(4+5\cos k)/(5+4\cos k) runs monotonically from +1+1 at k=0k=0 to −1-1 at k=πk=\pi, the kink bandwidth is 2​|JB​B−JA​B|=2​|r−1|​JA​B2|J_{BB}-J_{AB}|=2|r-1|J_{AB}, with the band minimum at k=πk=\pi for r<1r<1 and at k=0k=0 for r>1r>1.

The dimer point as a special case.

At r=1r=1 the deviation VV switches off, so εdom=0\varepsilon_{\rm dom}=0. Eq. (10) collapses to a flat kink band and Eq. (11) to EK+12​JA​B​(1+2​cos⁡k)E_{K}+\tfrac{1}{2}J_{AB}\,(1+2\cos k). This is also the one point where the absolute reference is exact, because the bare VBS is the true ground state, and the projector Rayleigh quotient supplies it directly. Only the antikink’s wall triangle carries spin-32\tfrac{3}{2} weight [h~k¯​(0)=34​JA​B\tilde{h}_{\overline{\rm k}}(0)=\tfrac{3}{4}J_{AB}, Eq. (40)], so

ωk​(k)=0,ωk¯​(k)=34​JA​Bo⁡(k)=(54+cos⁡k)​JA​B,\omega_{\rm k}(k)=0,\qquad\omega_{\overline{\rm k}}(k)=\frac{\tfrac{3}{4}J_{AB}}{o(k)}=\quantity(\tfrac 54+\cos k)J_{AB}, (43)

this is the Nakamura-Kubo dispersion [28, 37] with minimum 14​JA​B\tfrac{1}{4}J_{AB} at k=πk=\pi.

Anchoring the additive constant EKE_{K} to the ED spectral gap.

The closed forms (10)-(11) determine only energy differences, they are built entirely from the bulk-subtracted combination R⁡(d)R(d) [Eq. (38)], from which the entire kk-dependence follows, while the absolute on-site reference Eref=h⁡(0)/o⁡(0)E_{\rm ref}=h(0)/o(0) does not survive the construction. For r≠1r\neq 1 the true ground state is dressed and lies well below the bare VBS on which the wall states are built, so a wall creation energy measured from the VBS reference is unreliable near the phase boundaries. The excitation energies of the DSF, however, are measured from the true ground state. Since a single spinon is topological and never created alone, only the energy of the pair is observable, and the mismatch of references is absorbed into the single global constant EKE_{K}, fixed by matching the bottom of the two-spinon continuum to the true spectral gap,

minq⁡mink1​[εk​(k1)+εk¯​(q−k1)]=ΔED.\min_{q}\,\min_{k_{1}}\bigl[\varepsilon_{\rm k}(k_{1})+\varepsilon_{\overline{\rm k}}(q-k_{1})\bigr]=\Delta_{\rm ED}. (44)

Here ΔED\Delta_{\rm ED} is the singlet–triplet gap E0​(Stotz=1)−E0​(Stotz=0)E_{0}(S^{z}_{\rm tot}{=}1)-E_{0}(S^{z}_{\rm tot}{=}0) of the periodic chain. The lowest excitation reachable by an SzS^{z} probe, i.e. the same object whose onset the DSF measures. The first excitation within the Stotz=0S^{z}_{\rm tot}=0 sector is the near-degenerate second VBS singlet, which carries no DSF weight . The gap is computed by sparse Lanczos diagonalization for rings of N=4N=4-1212 unit cells and extrapolated linearly in 1/N1/N to the production size N=32N=32 (Fig. 9). At the exactly solvable point, the anchor reproduces the known antikink gap 0.215​JA​B0.215\,J_{AB} from the ED extrapolation  [28] and 0.2192​JA​B0.2192\,J_{AB} from the five-cluster variational bound  [37]. Everything else in the overlays (the shape of the edges, the continuum width, and the soft-mode migration) is then parameter-free.

D.4 Two-spinon continuum

The operator SqzS^{z}_{q} carries Δ​S=1\Delta S=1 and creates the walls only in pairs. A single spinon (spin 12\tfrac{1}{2}) is inaccessible within the excitation protocol. These two walls do not interact because of deconfinement, and the generalized eigen-problem (H−E0)​ψ=ω​𝒪​ψ(H-E_{0})\psi=\omega\,\mathcal{O}\psi factorizes. Labeling the pair by the two absolute wall positions |a,b⟩\ket{a,b} (kink at aa, antikink at bb), the separated-wall overlap and Hamiltonian are both products of independent single-wall sequences,

⟨a,b|a′,b′⟩\displaystyle\innerproduct{a,b}{a',b'} =o⁡(a−a′)​o​(b−b′),\displaystyle=o(a-a^{\prime})\,o(b-b^{\prime}), (45)
⟨a,b|⁡(H−E0)​|a′,b′⟩\displaystyle\bra{a,b}(H-E_{0})\ket{a',b'} =hk​(a−a′)​o​(b−b′)\displaystyle=h_{\rm k}(a-a^{\prime})\,o(b-b^{\prime})
+o⁡(a−a′)​hk¯​(b−b′),\displaystyle\quad+o(a-a^{\prime})\,h_{\overline{\rm k}}(b-b^{\prime}), (46)

with hk,hk¯h_{\rm k},h_{\overline{\rm k}} the single-wall hopping sequences. In the double-momentum basis |k1,k2⟩=∑a,bei​k1​a+i​k2​b​|a,b⟩\ket{k_1,k_2}=\sum_{a,b}e^{ik_{1}a+ik_{2}b}\ket{a,b} both matrices are diagonal, and the fixed-qq generalized eigen-problem collapses to the scalar relation hk​(k1)​o​(k2)+o⁡(k1)​hk¯​(k2)=ω​o​(k1)​o​(k2)h_{\rm k}(k_{1})\,o(k_{2})+o(k_{1})\,h_{\overline{\rm k}}(k_{2})=\omega\,o(k_{1})\,o(k_{2}). Dividing by o⁡(k1)​o​(k2)o(k_{1})o(k_{2}), the non-orthogonal metric cancels as a common factor leaving ω=εk​(k1)+εk¯​(k2)\omega=\varepsilon_{\rm k}(k_{1})+\varepsilon_{\overline{\rm k}}(k_{2}) with εwall​(k)=hwall​(k)/o⁡(k)\varepsilon_{\rm wall}(k)=h_{\rm wall}(k)/o(k) the single-wall Rayleigh quotients of Eqs. (10)-(11). Imposing the total momentum q=k1+k2q=k_{1}+k_{2} gives the cross-convolution of Eq. (9), the untruncated set of bands, with free relative motion ψq​(d)∼ei​k1​d\psi_{q}(d)\sim e^{ik_{1}d}. The qq-dependence of the continuum then reads off the closed forms, at the dimer point the flat kink [εdom=0\varepsilon_{\rm dom}=0, Eq. (43)] absorbs the total momentum at zero cost and the continuum sweeps the full antikink band [14,94]​JA​B[\tfrac{1}{4},\tfrac{9}{4}]J_{AB} at every qq. For r≠1r\neq 1 the dispersing kink constrains the pair and the soft mode of the lower edge migrates across the zone.

D.5 The two-kink structure factor

To obtain the distribution of spectral weight inside the continuum, we do a bruteforce diagonalization of the projected problem in the truncated two-wall space {|i,d⟩}\{\ket{i,d}\} (ii = kink cell, dd = kink-antikink separation, 0≤d≤D0\leq d\leq D). At fixed qq this is the generalized eigen-problem

H⁡(q)​ψn=ωn​𝒪​(q)​ψn,H(q)\,\psi_{n}=\omega_{n}\,\mathcal{O}(q)\,\psi_{n}, (47)

and, with the d=0d=0 magnon as the source, the structure factor is

Sz​z​(q,ω)=∑n|⟨d=0|​𝒪​(q)​|ψn⟩|2​δ​(ω−ωn).S^{zz}(q,\omega)=\sum_{n}\big|\bra{d{=}0}\mathcal{O}(q)\ket{\psi_n}\big|^{2}\,\delta\!\quantity(\omega-\omega_n). (48)

The numerical procedures mirrors the MPS-SMA of Appendix B.

  1. 1.

    Exact block elements. On an open window of Nw=16N_{w}=16 cells, build the two-wall product states |i,d⟩\ket{i,d}, 0≤d≤D0\leq d\leq D, centred on the window, and evaluate every Hamiltonian and overlap element by exact dense contraction,

    M⁡[Δ,d,d′]=⟨i,d|​H​|i+Δ,d′⟩,𝒪⁡[Δ,d,d′]=⟨i,d|i+Δ,d′⟩,\begin{split}M[\Delta,d,d^{\prime}]&=\bra{i,d}H\ket{i{+}\Delta,d'},\\ \mathcal{O}[\Delta,d,d^{\prime}]&=\innerproduct{i,d}{i{+}\Delta,d'},\end{split} (49)

    which depend only on (Δ,d,d′)(\Delta,d,d^{\prime}) by translation invariance in the window bulk. The elements decay geometrically with the wall shift [as the overlap (−12)|Δ|(-\tfrac{1}{2})^{|\Delta|}, Eq. (35)] and are kept for |Δ|≤4|\Delta|\leq 4, with both walls restricted to the bulk.

  2. 2.

    Momentum assembly. The centre-of-mass Fourier transform |q,d⟩=L−1/2∑iei​q​(i+d/2)|i,d⟩\ket{q,d}=L^{-1/2}\sum_{i}e^{iq(i+d/2)}\ket{i,d} turns the blocks into the (D+1)×(D+1)(D{+}1)\times(D{+}1) matrices

    H​(q)d​d′=∑Δei​q​Δ​ei​q​(d′−d)/2​M​[Δ,d,d′],H(q)_{dd^{\prime}}=\sum_{\Delta}e^{iq\Delta}\,e^{iq(d^{\prime}-d)/2}\,M[\Delta,d,d^{\prime}], (50)

    and identically 𝒪⁡(q)\mathcal{O}(q) from 𝒪⁡[Δ,d,d′]\mathcal{O}[\Delta,d,d^{\prime}]. The half-phase ei​q​(d′−d)/2e^{iq(d^{\prime}-d)/2} is a diagonal gauge that leaves the spectrum unchanged but renders both matrices Hermitian.

  3. 3.

    Canonical orthogonalization. The (−12)|d|(-\tfrac{1}{2})^{|d|} overlaps make the two-wall states nearly linearly dependent, so 𝒪⁡(q)\mathcal{O}(q) is near-singular and a Cholesky-based generalized solver fails. We therefore diagonalize the metric, 𝒪⁡(q)=U​diag​(s)​U†\mathcal{O}(q)=U\,\mathrm{diag}(s)\,U^{\dagger}, discard the directions with si≤τ​maxj⁡(sj)s_{i}\leq\tau\max_{j}(s_{j}) (τ=10−8\tau=10^{-8}; typically one direction at D=6D=6), build X=Udiag(s)−1/2X=U\,\mathrm{diag}(s)^{-1/2} on the kept directions [so that X†​𝒪​(q)​X=𝟙X^{\dagger}\mathcal{O}(q)X=\mathbbm{1}], solve the standard Hermitian problem for X†​H​(q)​XX^{\dagger}H(q)X, and map the eigenvectors back as ψn=X​ϕn\psi_{n}=X\phi_{n}, which are 𝒪\mathcal{O}-normalized.

  4. 4.

    Source weights The basis is non-orthogonal, the overlap with the source is taken in the metric, wn=|(𝒪⁡(q)​ψn)0|2w_{n}=|(\mathcal{O}(q)\psi_{n})_{0}|^{2} [the weight of Eq. (48)]; the total weight at each qq, ∑nwn=𝒪​(q)00\sum_{n}w_{n}=\mathcal{O}(q)_{00} up to the discarded null directions, is conserved and merely redistributed over the bands.

  5. 5.

    Energy reference. Energies are measured from the window VBS energy E0E_{0}. At r=1r=1 the VBS is the true ground state and the spectrum is used as is. For r≠1r\neq 1 the bands are shifted rigidly so that the D=6D=6 continuum floor coincides with the extrapolated gap ΔED\Delta_{\rm ED} of Eq. (44), the same anchor used for the closed-form dispersions.

The truncation yields D+1D{+}1 bands that densify into the continuum as D→∞D\to\infty. The D=0D=0 term is the coincident pair, i.e. exactly the triplon of Appendix C. Increasing DD lets the pair delocalize and redistributes the weight downward from ω=JA​B\omega=J_{AB} toward the two-spinon gap.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
